ועוד דאם המחיצות מועילים כו' ר"ל אם המחיצות גורמים לאסור כל החלל איך לא יגרמו לאסור את המחיצות עצמם:
מדפריך מרב' דאמר כצ"ל. ועיין הג"מ במ"א ס"ק ה'. הא המחיצות מפסיקים. ר"ל אי סתם ב"ה שבזמן הש"ס היה עם מחיצות. משא"כ רבא דקאי אצואה דליכ' הפסק מחיצה א"ו דסתם ב"ה שלהם לא ה"ל מחיצות ופריך שפיר. וא"ל דמאי דייק הרב"י דאי ב"ה שבזמן הש"ס ה"ל מחיצות מאי פריך מרב' ארפרם הא רפרם מיירי בי"ל מחיצות וא"כ המחיצות מפסיקים הא אי אמרי' דבזמן הש"ס ה"ל מחיצות ע"כ אפי' מחיצות לא הוי הפסק וע"כ לא אמר הרב"י דמחיצות מפסיקים אלא משום דהוכיח לפ"ד דבזמן הש"ס לא היה לב"ה מחיצות ולכך הצריכו הרחק' מב"ה אבל כשיש לו מחיצה אמרינן מסבר' דמפסיק וא"כ מאי ראיה מייתי הרב"י דלמ' לעולם בזמן הש"ס ה"ל מחיצות ואפ"ה פריך שפיר מרב' על רפרם דניהו דרפרם מיירי בי"ל מחיצות הא המחיצות לא הוי הפסק א"ו דבזמן הש"ס ה"ל מחיצות מ"מ דייק הרב"י ניהו דאי בזמן הש"ס ה"ל מחיצות אז אין המחיצות מפסיקי' אבל מ"מ מנ"ל למקשן להקשות מרב' הא רבא מיירי בלא מחיצות ורפרם מיירי במחיצות ודלמ' המחיצות מפסיקים:

machatzit_hashekel.en:
(siman kuf alef) If he has partitions — even if they are not ten [tefachim] high; and Bach inferred thus from Shulchan Aruch's wording, since it was left unstated and wrote "if he has partitions" without specifying ten [tefachim] high — it implies even less than ten helps according to the Ri, as he wrote in his long work; for it seemed to him, etc., they do not help even for ten high; and it suffices if we are lenient like Bach for ten high, but not for less — as Magen Avraham concludes at the end of this siman kuf alef.
New privy, etc. The ground is forbidden even though there is no feces in it, through designation for the need of the privy; likewise partitions — even though there is no feces on them — are graf shel rei, namely the vessel in which feces rests, as below seif 7.
Partitions between him and the privy, and the plain meaning, etc., on the one who says thus — as explained above seif 6 seif 4: he put his hand into a hole of the privy, and on this Rashi and Baal HaMaor [explain]: partitions between him and between the privy, etc. And likewise in Rashba's novellae on the above gemara "he put his hand into the privy" — and we say thus, etc. For it teaches "one who enters" — when he has partitions it does not mean entering; and if so, even though it says to him "partitions," it must be at a distance of four amot; it implies partitions do not help.
However, this "if he has" means even if he has no partitions, the language "one who enters" applies — namely, he entered that field in which the privy is within it; and such we learned in tractate Taharot chapter 6 mishnah 5: one who enters a valley in the rainy season.
For we do not call it a privy except the place of sitting — for more than the house of sitting one cannot recite [Shema] in the privy; what boundary did he establish to recite [Shema] in the privy since he has no partitions? If so, in a new [privy] it is permitted to recite within the partitions, etc. — for in a new one only its inside is forbidden but outside it, opposite it, is permitted, as seif 2 wrote; and if so, if there were no partitions, it would not be forbidden in a new one except on the place of sitting, which alone is called privy and no more; and if so, when he has partitions, only the place of sitting is forbidden, but opposite it — even within the partitions — is permitted, for the partitions do not cause prohibition more than if he had no partitions.
Ravina from Nedarim. And this is from here in siman 53, and it is explained there in Nedarim that Ravina had two inquiries: one — they designated a privy: does designation help? And if you say designation helps, he must inquire whether there is "hand" to the privy — namely, if he said "this house shall be a privy" and "this too." And certainly the second too is a privy, except that he said about the second "and this" and did not say the word "too," so it is only "hand" — for the law is not clear whether he meant "and this" shall be a privy and "this" for ordinary use, and it is not resolved; and if so, what Magen Avraham wrote "and this too — what?" — the word "too" is an error, for in such a case he would not need it at all, and it is plain to him that he meant for the privy and it is forbidden; only if he did not say the word "too" would he need it, as above.
With this, ordinary use does not apply — for the place of sitting is not fit for anything else except the privy.
And if he has partitions — it is forbidden to recite, etc. — and not as Magen Avraham wrote above; rather, the partitions reduce — namely, when he has no partitions he is not forbidden in a new one except the place of sitting, for more than that one cannot recite [Shema] in the privy; what boundary did he establish? Shall the whole world recite [Shema] in the privy? Not so: when he has partitions, then on the contrary the partitions limit, and we say: all that is within the partitions is called privy. And if so, Ravina's inquiry is in a new privy in which he has partitions and said "this" — whether he meant all that is in the space of the partitions shall be privy, or the space is for another use.
If so, what does the gemara in Berachos chapter Mi sheMeto challenge — that Ravina should resolve his inquiry that designation does not help for a privy, and a new privy is permitted? For Rephaim [in the name] of R' Chisda said: a person stands opposite the privy and prays — and they establish it there in Berachos that perforce Rephaim deals with a new privy and permits opposite it even though before him in an old privy it is forbidden as far as his eyes can see, and nevertheless he permits opposite it in a new one; perforce designation is not a [significant] matter and it has no law of privy. And they answer: Ravina's inquiry is regarding its inside, and Rephaim deals outside it, where it is permitted in a new one — the gemara's words are brought in Magen Avraham siman kuf hei; and Magen Avraham's view is: that which the questioner does not bring the gemara's answer — for perforce Rephaim deals outside it, for it teaches "opposite it"; perforce the presumption was that Ravina's inquiry too was outside it, until the answerer innovated for him that Ravina deals specifically inside it. And now that perforce the second inquiry is regarding "hand" when he said "and this" — it deals when he has partitions, as Magen Avraham wrote — for otherwise ordinary use would not be needed. If so, the first inquiry too — whether designation helps for a privy — deals when he has partitions, for the two inquiries are asked together; if so, since it deals with one who has partitions, perforce he would not need to ask only its inside, but outside it is certainly permitted — for even in an old one partitions help to be a separation and it is permitted outside according to the Ri; and since Ravina perforce deals inside it and Rephaim's wording implies he deals outside it, since he said the language "opposite it," as Magen Avraham wrote siman kuf hei — if so, perhaps he deals with one who has no partitions, as plain privies were in the time of the gemara according to the Ri; and if so, the gemara's answer is explained: Rephaim deals outside and Ravina inside — if so, what is the challenge, and how did it not bring the gemara's answer? See in Magen Avraham siman kuf hei.
And further: if partitions help, etc. — meaning, if partitions cause the whole space to be forbidden, how will they not cause the partitions themselves to be forbidden?
From the challenge on Rava who said, etc. See Hagahot Maimoniyot in Magen Avraham siman kuf hei: behold, partitions interrupt. Meaning, if a plain privy in the time of the gemara had partitions. Not so Rava, who stands at feces where there is no interruption of a partition — or that their plain privy had no partitions — and he challenged well. And if he has partitions — why did the Ri infer: if a privy in the time of the gemara had partitions, what does Rava challenge on Rephaim? Rephaim deals with one who has partitions — if so, partitions interrupt; but if we say that in the time of the gemara there were partitions, perforce even partitions would not be an interruption — and perforce the Ri did not say partitions interrupt except because he proved to his view that in the time of the gemara privies had no partitions, and therefore distancing from the privy was required; but when he has a partition, we say it is reasonable that it interrupts. If so, what proof does the Ri bring — that perhaps always in the time of the gemara there were partitions, and nevertheless he challenged well Rava on Rephaim — that Rephaim deals with one who has partitions: behold, partitions are not an interruption; or that in the time of the gemara there were partitions — nevertheless the Ri inferred thus: if in the time of the gemara there were partitions, then partitions do not interrupt; but nevertheless, whence does the questioner challenge Rava? Rava deals without partitions and Rephaim with partitions — and perhaps partitions interrupt.
And whence does he challenge that there is no feces in it? This is the gemara's first answer — and why did we not bring the questioner up [to it]? Because he knew to challenge on this as he challenged afterward on this answer; and "R' Yirmiyah: privy — they said that even when there is no feces in it" — if so, Taz too should not have been inclined to distinguish that Rephaim deals with interruption of partitions, for he knew the truth that partitions do not interrupt — as above.
It should appear they are ten [tefachim] high. Then one may rely on Bach as above; and see Taz, who also agreed partitions do not interrupt — except he wrote specifically when that partition is designated for the privy alone; but if it is designated for the house and the privy — e.g. he uses one side for the house and the other side for the privy — it does not have the law of privy partitions, and it is permitted to recite even near it.
Forbidden according to all. Even according to the one who says in siman 79 that a partition interrupts even for smell — nevertheless privy partitions are inferior for this matter.

mishnah_berurah.en:
(1) It is forbidden to read - Meaning, before it as far as his eyes can see, and behind him four amot. If there is a foul odor there, he must distance four amot from the place where the odor ceases.
(2) It was cleared out - Its prohibition is from the Torah, since this place was formerly normally used for excrement and therefore "your camp" is not holy. Accordingly, if one is uncertain whether it is an old privy or a new one, we rule stringently, like every doubt concerning excrement above in siman 76 seif 7.
(3) When it has no partitions - Such as behind a fence or behind houses. It is obvious that even if they did not initially designate that place as a privy, since people are accustomed to relieve themselves there it is called an old privy. A proof is from above siman 42, where the poskim wrote that if one always uses a cloth to wrap tefillin, it is forbidden to use it for another purpose as though he had designated it; see there.
(4) Partitions - It appears that this is speaking where they reach the ground, or at least within three tefachim of the ground, where we apply lavud; otherwise it is forbidden according to Rav Hai Gaon cited in Beit Yosef siman 87; see there.
(5) Does not reach - If the foul odor reaches him, it is forbidden until he distances four amot from where the odor ceases; this suffices even in front of him according to the Mechaber. Know that the Mechaber's view is to permit even with partitions that are not ten high, as stated in Beit Yosef, but all the later authorities disagree with him on this. With partitions ten high, some later authorities hold like him, while many later authorities disagree even in this. Their reason is that since the partitions are designated to receive excrement, we judge them like excrement and like a chamber pot below in siman 87, which is forbidden even without a foul odor. From the words of the Gra in his Biur it also appears that his view is to be stringent, and so Peri Megadim, Derech HaChayim, and many other recent later authorities are all stringent. They hold that one must distance four amot from the partitions, and before him as far as his eyes can see, even if the excrement was cleared out and there is no foul odor. Therefore one must be careful not to read, pray, or speak words of Torah in a courtyard opposite a privy as far as his eyes can see, even if it is closed and the excrement inside cannot be seen. It is therefore proper to be careful, when making a sukkah in a courtyard, to do it in such a way that the walls of the privy are not directly opposite the sukkah entrance when it is open, for then he would need to be careful when speaking words of Torah and other sacred matters. Likewise, if there is a privy opposite the window of his house, and the window is open and he stands in his house facing the privy, it is proper to be careful not to speak words of Torah then. Nevertheless, in pressing circumstances one may rely on leniency if no foul odor reaches him, for there is a double doubt: the Beit Yosef and Bach in this siman permit with partitions ten high, and the Rosh in siman 79 seif 2 permits even with excrement when it is in another domain although he sees it. Closing his eyes is effective according to all opinions in such a case. The later authorities further wrote that our stringency regarding privy partitions, judging them externally like excrement, applies specifically to partitions made only for the privy, such as when one made a special room for this in a courtyard. But if he built along a wall of a house, so that the same wall is actually a wall of the privy, that wall does not have the law of a privy for this matter, and one may read even near it, since the partition is not designated exclusively for the privy.

yad_ephraim.en: (In Magen Avraham, note 8) Opposite the seat area, etc. — it appears his intent is that he holds: certainly if moist it is forbidden only the seat area. If so, when one said plainly "this house for a bathroom" and did not designate the seat area, the house is not forbidden at all in such a case — there is no designation; therefore he designates the seat area and points to a place that this shall be the bathroom seat area. If so, when he said regarding the second "and this house" it is difficult: either he did not designate a place for it — then in any case it is not forbidden at all; or he points to a place and says "this place" — then one must again be uncertain: perhaps he meant for ordinary use; perhaps he saw this place clearly and said it is for another use, for the whole house is for another use and not a bathroom — rather necessarily what he points to in a special place in the house and says about it "and this place" is to designate it as the seat area. And again Magen Avraham wrote: he answered that with partitions it is forbidden to recite inside; if so, what is the question, etc. — meaning in Berachos he challenges from Ravina's question: if one designated it for a bathroom, what is its law, against R' Chanina who said a person stands in a bathroom and prays; and the Gemara answers there: to stand inside to pray, but opposite is permitted, as written in note 5. And for the questioner it must be that it seemed to him that Ravina's question too regarding opposite deals with inside — it seems obvious it is forbidden; rather necessarily "opposite" needs to be asked, and it is difficult for him from R' Chanina. And now it is difficult: what is the question — even if we say Ravina's question is not literally about the seat area, which is certainly forbidden, nevertheless one may well say Ravina: although he said plainly "designated for a bathroom," it deals when there are partitions, similar to designating a bathhouse, and he asks whether it is permitted to recite within the partitions opposite the seat area, or perhaps within partitions in such a case is forbidden; and R' Chanina who permits opposite deals when there are no partitions. With this there is no reason to say the questioner erred and thought this law obvious to forbid, and they answered that there it means to stand inside — and he needs to ask whether within partitions is like within the seat area, for why should this be obvious to the questioner? And also accordingly they should have answered: there it deals within partitions and opposite the seat area — but certainly it deals in an old one with partitions too, and there is no difference between inside partitions and outside the partition. And what Magen Avraham wrote further: if partitions help, etc. — at first glance requires study what this has to do with that; and it appears he means: granted, if partitions do not help in a new one regarding inside, then one could say in an old one it is permitted opposite, for the surrounding partitions are not part of the waste body; whereas if we say partitions help for the waste body to forbid all inside partitions — because partitions are made for their interior — whence do we lighten in an old one opposite, lest it be like a cesspool receptacle? And what Magen Avraham wrote: it should challenge the Beit Yosef's question, "and according to your view," etc. — at first glance requires study, for in truth the Gemara answered it deals so; and it appears Magen Avraham holds: granted, if a bathroom has partitions it is reasonable that the questioner deals when there is feces in it and nevertheless it is permitted opposite the partitions, and on this it answers it deals when there is no feces; whereas if we say the bathroom has no partitions, then necessarily the bathroom R' Chanina mentions is one without feces, for otherwise why mention bathroom at all, since the main stringency of a bathroom is because of feces; and if R' Chanina comes to permit when there is feces, it should have said a person stands opposite feces and prays — why mention bathroom? Rather necessarily the questioner too knew it deals when there is no feces; if so there is no question on Rava. And this is Magen Avraham's intent writing it should challenge, "and according to your view, perhaps even though it has no partitions nevertheless it deals when there is no feces" — meaning for him it is reasonable that the questioner thought a plain bathroom has feces, unlike Beit Yosef who necessarily deals when there is feces in it (and Magen Avraham's wording "perhaps" means: perhaps since it deals without feces therefore it is more lenient than feces itself). And one may also say Magen Avraham holds it is not reasonable to say the questioner did not know one could establish it without feces, for certainly the term bathroom applies also without feces (and the wording "perhaps" Magen Avraham wrote is literal); but certainly the questioner too knew this R' Chanina deals without feces, only he holds bathroom law and feces law are equivalent and he did not hold to distinguish between them, as Rav Yosef actually holds here; and he holds that R' Chanina mentioned bathroom to inform us that opposite is permitted but inside is forbidden even without feces, but opposite is at least permitted even though it has feces law; therefore he challenges Ravina and the answer holds there is a difference between a bathroom without feces and one with feces, and he challenges from Rav Yosef; if so, whence does the questioner hold reasonably that partitions too are like a cesspool receptacle and have feces law, and therefore partition interruption does not help.

However, this is specifically regarding partitions that are made only for the privy — e.g. when one makes in his courtyard a room designated only for this — but if he adjoined the privy to the partitions of the house, even though that partition is literally the privy partition, it is permitted to recite [Shema] even nearby, since the partition is not designated for the privy alone; and all this is in a privy that has no pit but the feces rests on the ground.

kaf_hachayim.en: (b) There — it is forbidden to recite [Shema] opposite an old privy. Even if they washed it, cleaned it, and coated it with lime — nevertheless, since an hour has passed, it has no allowance. Beit Yehudah chelek 1 Orach Chayyim siman 10. See in Mishna Berurah siman 84 in Biur Halacha ot 1, Chasam Sofer ot 1. But if he reconsidered regarding the privy and demolished it and made the place a house, it is permitted — for the reason is on account of disgrace; and since the name of privy was uprooted from it, there is no further disgrace — go out and see how the public treats it. And likewise in responsum of Peri Megadim regarding a bathhouse. Chasam Sofer there. See below siman 84 ot 3.

אך דבס"ד היה ניחא שהיה סובר דמיירי ביש בו צואה וא"כ הדין פשוט במשנה שצריך להרחיק ד"א ורפרם כחא דהיתיר' אתי לאשמעינן שאע"פ שעומד כנגדו יכול להתפלל וא"צ מלא עיניו אבל למאי דמשני באין בו צואה א"כ א"א לפרש דר"ל דמרחיק ד"א כיון שעדיין לא נזכר בשום מקום לאסור כשאין בו צואה להרחיק ד"א עד שיצטרך לו' דעכ"פ ע"י הרחקה שרי וע"כ דכוונת רפרם לאשמעי' דאף בלא הרחקה נמי שרי וכמו דקי"ל באמת למסקנ' דמוקי בחדתי ובתוכו דוקא אסור וכנגדו שרי והיינו בלא הרחקה א"כ אף למאי דמוקי אף באין בו צואה משמע דאף סמוך לבה"כ ממש שרי ואהא פריך מדר"י וליכא למימר דרב יוסף קאי אמתני' (ר"ל אהא דאתמר שירחיק מן הצואה ד"א אהא איתא דגם בב"ה הדין כן וקאמר רב יוסף עלה דב"ה שאמרו אע"פ שאין בו צואה) דהיינו ע"י שיעור ד"א דנהי דנימא הכי ומ"מ לפום הך תירוצ' א"צ לרפרם להרחיק כלל ולפ"ז הדר' קושית המג"א לדוכתי' מאי מספק' ליה לרבינ' תפשוט מדרפרם. אמנם נראה דבלא"ה קשה דתפשוט ליה מדרב יוסף דאמר ב"ה שאמרו אעפ"י שאין בו צואה משמע שעכ"פ היה בה אלא שעתה אין בו ותיפוק ליה דאפי' בחדתי שמעולם לא היו בו אסור וא"ל דבישן פשיט' ליה ובחדש מספק' ליה א"כ גם מדרפרם ליכא למפשט מידי דדלמא כנגדו פשיטא ליה ובתוכו מספק' ליה. אלא ודאי שז"א וכמ"ש המג"א שדוחק לומר דרפרם גופ' מספקא ליה. וא"כ תפשוט ליה מדרב יוסף וצ"ל דבהך צד האיבעי' דחדתי אסור י"ל דרב יוסף באמת קאי על דין צואה לפניו ג"כ שצריך מלא עיניו וע"ז קאמר דה"ה ב"ה שאין בו צואה משא"כ בחדתי עכ"פ א"צ מלא עיניו אבל לעולם הרחקה ד"א בעינן ולפ"ז נהי דנימא דרפרם ס"ל כסברת רב יוסף דב"ה שיש בו צואה ואין בו צואה שוים הם וד' אמות בעינן ולכך לא הזכיר בדבריו ד"א מ"מ קשה דהא אם נא' דרפרם סמך ע"ז דשוה אין בו צואה לצואה כסברת רב יוסף א"כ במלא עיניו הדין כן כמו לרב יוסף ולמה מתיר רפרם כנגדו דהא הך סבר' דרב יוסף yad_ephraim.en: (Magen Avraham, note 5) And one must say Ravina is uncertain — perhaps R' Perem deals with an old bathroom, etc. One should wonder: if so, why indeed did they not answer that Rav Yosef refers to the mishnah? And it appears because at first glance it is difficult: why did R' Perem not mention in his words that one must distance four amot — but per our way of learning it was reasonable that he thought it deals when there is feces in it; if so the law is obvious in the mishnah that one must distance four amot, and R' Perem as a leniency comes to inform us that even though one stands opposite it one may pray and need not distance as far as the eye can see. But per what they answer when there is no feces — then it is impossible to explain he meant distancing four amot, since nowhere yet was it mentioned to forbid when there is no feces to distance four amot, until one must say: at any rate through distancing it is permitted; and therefore R' Perem's intent is to inform that even without distancing it is also permitted. And as we actually hold in the conclusion: they establish it in a new one — inside specifically forbidden, opposite permitted — namely without distancing. If so, even per what they establish even without feces, it implies even adjacent to the bathroom itself is permitted; and on this he challenges from Rav Yosef. And one cannot say Rav Yosef refers to the mishnah (meaning on what was said that one distances four amot from feces — there it is found that the same law applies to a bathroom, and Rav Yosef says about it: a bathroom that they designated even though there is no feces in it) — that is through the measure of four amot; although one could say so, nevertheless per this answer R' Perem need not distance at all; and therefore Magen Avraham's question returns to its place: why is Ravina uncertain — let him resolve from R' Perem. However, it appears that otherwise it is difficult: let him resolve from Rav Yosef who said a bathroom that they designated even though there is no feces — implying there was feces in it but now there is not; and let him derive that even in a new one where there never was feces it is forbidden; and they answered that in an old one it is obvious to him and in a new one he is uncertain. If so, from R' Perem too one cannot resolve anything — perhaps opposite is obvious to him and inside he is uncertain. Rather certainly this is so, and as Magen Avraham wrote strained to say R' Perem himself is uncertain. If so, let him resolve from Rav Yosef; and one must say on that side of the question that a new one is forbidden: Rav Yosef actually refers to feces law before it too requiring as far as the eye can see, and on this he says the same for a bathroom without feces, unlike a new one where at least one need not distance as far as the eye can see — but always four amot are required. And therefore although we could say R' Perem holds like Rav Yosef's view that a bathroom with feces and without feces are equivalent and four amot are required, and therefore he did not mention four amot in his words — nevertheless it is difficult: for if we say R' Perem relied on this that without feces equals feces per Rav Yosef, then for as far as the eye can see the law is likewise as Rav Yosef — why does R' Perem permit opposite, for this view of Rav Yosef deals regarding as far as the eye can see, whereas for four amot one need not say in a new one too there is prohibition — Ravina's question should be on one side only; and necessarily it deals with as far as the eye can see, and therefore he properly challenges from Rav Yosef on R' Perem. But Ravina properly is uncertain that perhaps a new one is permitted and Rav Yosef refers to the mishnah that even though there is no feces one needs four amot, for it is equivalent for this matter to the law when there is feces — but a new one is entirely permitted, and R' Perem deals without feces. Nevertheless four amot are required — this is obvious to R' Perem: for distancing four amot, without feces equals with feces; only regarding as far as the eye can see he says one may distinguish that without feces a person stands opposite and prays. Further it appears to me per the above path, somewhat differently, in explanation of Magen Avraham's words in siman 83, note 5, who wrote Ravina is uncertain — perhaps it deals with an old one, etc. — for at first glance one should wonder: why indeed did they not answer Rav Yosef refers to the mishnah, and why did they need to answer in a new one; and also whence did the questioner challenge? And it appears to me that at first glance it is difficult otherwise on Magen Avraham's words: how is it possible to say R' Perem deals with an old bathroom without feces — for then it implies distancing four amot is not needed either. Granted for what he thought, that it deals when there is feces in it, Magen Avraham properly wrote he cannot challenge from the mishnah, for one could say R' Perem deals when he distanced four amot because the law is obvious in the mishnah that four amot from feces are required, and R' Perem as leniency comes to inform that even opposite one stands and prays and need not distance as far as the eye can see. Whereas if it deals without feces, this law was not yet mentioned in the mishnah, and from R' Perem's plain wording it implies even four amot are not needed — then although we could say Rav Yosef refers to the mishnah, nevertheless distancing four amot is in any case required, and it is difficult on R' Perem; and therefore it deals, etc.; and Magen Avraham's question returns regarding the Mordechai. And one must say the Mordechai, according to Magen Avraham's intent in his words, holds that what R' Perem said — a person stands opposite a bathroom, etc. — this is as explained that four amot distancing is required, for less than four amot is not called opposite but inside; and therefore what the Gemara answers — Ravina needs to ask to pray inside, opposite is permitted — means at a distance of four amot, for even in a new one four amot are required; only Ravina asks whether opposite is permitted or whether as far as the eye can see is required like other bathrooms without feces. And now one can say he cannot answer Rav Yosef refers to the mishnah; and regarding distancing four amot it was stated: if so, it is difficult — resolve Ravina's question, for from Rav Yosef it implies specifically in a bathroom without feces four amot are required, but at least there was feces in it before and they removed it; but a new one does not even need four amot, for otherwise Rav Yosef should have informed us more that even in a new one distancing is required; and the questioner thought Ravina's question regarding opposite is whether distancing is required, and he should have proven this from Rav Yosef. Rather necessarily Rav Yosef deals regarding as far as the eye can see, that it is required even though there is no feces, and through this a new one is permitted; but four amot perhaps require distancing — and if so it is difficult on R' Perem who said one need not distance as far as the eye can see; and they answered nevertheless they established Ravina's question inside specifically, but opposite is permitted — why did they need to establish R' Perem in a new one; let us say R' Perem deals with an old one and Rav Yosef refers to the mishnah; and nevertheless resolve Ravina regarding inside — this is so, for as I already wrote: what does the answer mean, Ravina needs to ask to pray inside — not literally inside itself, but also within four amot is called inside per the Mordechai's view; and opposite that is permitted is outside four amot. If so, from Rav Yosef it is proven that specifically in a bathroom without feces four amot are required, whereas a new one does not need four amot — and automatically Ravina's question is resolved that it is not reasonable to distinguish between inside itself and outside four amot; and the Gemara in conclusion properly distinguishes between inside and opposite: for an old one as far as the eye can see is required, and in a new one not. But per our way of learning, even in an old one one need not distance except four amot — if so, in a new one too if we say inside is forbidden, obviously four amot are required. Rather necessarily Rav Yosef deals regarding as far as the eye can see, and they had to establish R' Perem in a new one. Unlike Magen Avraham who properly says Ravina's question is not obvious stringently from R' Perem who said opposite — implying outside four amot, as far as the eye can see permitted, whereas inside forbidden — because he holds perhaps in a new one even inside is permitted, and R' Perem deals even with an old one, and Rav Yosef refers to the mishnah; for now that we stand that a new one is permitted inside, Rav Yosef can properly refer to the mishnah — and specifically in an old one without feces distancing is required, but a new one even inside is permitted; and this is Ravina's question: if a new one is forbidden, then R' Perem deals with a new one and only opposite is permitted but inside forbidden. Or perhaps R' Perem deals with an old one and Rav Yosef likewise, and specifically in an old one it is forbidden but a new one permitted; and then the Mordechai who rules the question leniently — accordingly R' Perem deals, and what he said to permit opposite is through distancing — or as Rav Yosef said.

eliyah_rabbah.he: [ד] אבל לא בתוכו וכו'. כן כתב בית יוסף משום שהרמב"ם והרא"ש פסקו הכי וכן כתב רבינו ירוחם בשם הרא"ש. ומה שתמה בית יוסף על רבינו ירוחם שכתב אחר כך דהרא"ש פסק להקל, עיינתי בדברי רבינו ירוחם ולא קשה מידי דכוונתו שהרא"ש פירש דברי רי"ף שכתב שהוא בעיא דלא איפשטא סתם ופירשו הרא"ש לקולא, אבל הרא"ש לדידיה סבירא ליה להחמיר לזה ברור עיין שם כי קיצרתי. וכן בעל הלכות גדולות מחמיר ואפילו בדיעבד אם כבר קרא או התפלל לא יצא והיינו מדרבנן ונפקא מינה לענין ספיקא ועיין תשובת ר' יום טוב צהלון סימן ע"ב. ונראה דכמו שאסרו בתוכו הוא הדין דאסור תוך ארבע אמות דידיה דהא רב חסדא אמר עומד אדם בבית הכסא ומתפלל ופירש רש"י שם רחוק ארבע אמות, אף דיש לומר דפירש כן למקשן מסתמא הוא הדין למסקנא, דהא סלקא דעתך דש"ס דאפילו בתר שאסור כמלא עיניו, אם כן למסקנא די לנו שנתיר כמלא עיניו אבל תוך ארבע אמות אסור וכן כתב הדרישה להדיא בשם המרדכי. ונראה קצת ראיה לזה מדנקט לשון כנגד ולא קאמר עומד בצדו ומתפלל כדאיתא בדף כ"ה ע"א אם היה גבוה עשרה יושב בצדו וקורא אלא על כרחך דוקא רחוק ארבע אמות מותר. וצריך עיון דמשמעות הטור ושולחן ערוך ולבוש לכאורה דאין צריך הרחקה כלל, ועיין לעיל סימן פ"א, ולדינא אפשר להקל בדיעבד:
eliyah_rabbah.en: [4] But not inside it, etc. So wrote Beit Yosef because Rambam and Rosh ruled thus, and Rabbeinu Yeruham wrote in the name of Rosh. What Beit Yosef wondered about Rabbeinu Yeruham — that he later wrote the Rosh ruled leniently — I examined Rabbeinu Yeruham's words and there is no difficulty: his intent is that Rosh explained Rif's words, who wrote it is an unresolved matter in general and Rosh explained it leniently; but Rosh himself holds it is clear to be stringent — see there, for I abbreviated. And likewise Baal Halakhot Gedolot is stringent, and even after the fact if one already read or prayed he has not fulfilled [his obligation] — that is, it is rabbinic; and this has bearing for a case of doubt. See responsum of R' Yom Tov Tzahalon siman 72. And it appears that just as they forbade inside it, so too it is forbidden within his four amot — for Rav Chisda said: a person stands in the privy and prays, and Rashi explained there: distant four amot. Although one could say he explained thus for the questioner, from the plain implication that is the law for the conclusion — for it could enter your mind the gemara [means] even afterward one must distance as far as his eyes can see; if so, for the conclusion it would suffice for us to permit as far as his eyes can see, but within four amot is forbidden — and Derishah wrote explicitly in the name of Mordechai. Some slight support for this: it uses the language "opposite" and does not say "standing at his side and praying" as appears on daf 25a — "if it were ten high, one sits at his side and reads" — rather, perforce one must say specifically distant four amot is permitted. (d) There — but if he has partitions, etc. Since it did not write how high the partition must be, it implies even if it is not ten [tefachim] high, as Beit Yosef wrote. However, Bach wrote that we require a partition ten [tefachim] high — see there; and likewise Knesset HaGedolah in Biur Halacha ot 3, Peri Chadash ot 1, Etz Chaim ot 2. Yet the view of Taz in siman kuf alef is to forbid even with a partition ten [tefachim] high, since the partitions are designated to receive feces — they are considered like feces — even though there is no bad smell there; see there. And likewise Magen Avraham in siman kuf alef. And Beit Din, Eliyah Rabbah ot 2, and likewise Shaarei Teshuvah ot 1, Rav Zundel ot 1, Chayei Adam kelal 3 ot 11, Chasam Sofer ot 2, Ruach Chaim siman 79 ot 2 — and specifically regarding partitions that are made only for the privy, e.g. when one makes in his courtyard a room designated for this alone; but if he built the privy in a partition of the house that he adjoined to that partition — even though that partition is literally the privy partition — that partition does not have the law of a privy for this matter, and it is permitted to recite [Shema] even nearby, since the partition is not designated for the privy alone. And from this: whoever has a privy in his courtyard in a designated room — one may not recite Shema or pray in the courtyard as far as opposite the privy as far as his eyes can see, like the law of feces; and this is in a privy that has no pit but the feces rests on the ground, like those in the days of the Sages of the Talmud at the edge of the field. Taz there. Eliyah Rabbah there, Shaarei Teshuvah there, Rav Zundel there, Chayei Adam there, Chasam Sofer there, Ruach Chaim there — and see there in Chasam Sofer that he was uncertain if there is a pit but it is under the drain and is not ten deep; and moreover even if it is not lacking that there is feces and urine outside — it is possible this too is considered like graf shel rei and it is forbidden to recite opposite it, as Beit Yosef wrote to this effect. See Ruach Chaim there and Ben Ish Chai parashat Bo ot 25. And all this if no bad smell reaches him; but if bad smell reaches him, it is forbidden according to all — for partitions do not help for smell. Magen Avraham there, Chayei Adam there, Chasam Sofer there. See what I wrote above siman 79 ot 19 and ot 21.

(d) Toilet rooms adjoining a synagogue — if they have partitions ten [tefachim] high and they also pray in the synagogue surrounded by partitions — we have no concern for these two separations, provided no bad smell reaches them. Shvut Yaakov chelek 1 siman 13. But if bad smell reaches them, there is no separation and a change of domain does not help, and neighbors must distance even though they have held it for many years — Or HaNe'elam book 5, and Beit Din Ikkei HaDat siman 5 ot 15. See further below siman 86 ot 3.

והוי כאלו מפורש בש"ס דלמסקנ' מיירי רפרם בישן וא"ב צואה וא"כ לדידן דקי"ל האיבעי' לחומר' מספק א"כ ה"ה די"ל דגם למסקנ' נשאר תי' הש"ס דרפרם מיירי בחדתי. אבל ישן אפי' א"ב צואה צ"ל לפניו כמל' עיניו כמו שתי' תחלה דמהיכי תיתי נמציא קול' חדשה באין הכרח. ואכתי צ"ב לפ"ז דע"כ צ"ל דהמקשן לא אסיק אדעתי' לחלק בדיני ב"ה והוי ס"ל בכל דבר או שי"ל דין ב"ה לכל דיניו וחומרותיו או אין לו דין ב"ה כלל א"כ מאי מקשה מ"א בס"ק א' עמ"ש מ"א וז"ל וא"ל דאם י"ל מחיצות אסור לקרות בתוכו אפי' מחדש. א"כ מאי פריך בגמ' דלמ' ר"ח מיירי כו' ורבינ' כו'. הא המקשן הוי ס"ל דאי תוכו אסור גם בחוץ אסור וא"כ ניהו דר"ח מיירי בלא מחיצות מ"מ ראוי לאסור כמל' עיניו כדין ב"ה ישן דהא המקשן הוי ס"ל דאין לחלק בדיני ב"ה כנ"ל ז"א דכאן כ' מ"א סבר' דנפשי' לפ' דברי מרדכי כפי מה שנ"ל דלא כהרב"י אבל בס"ק א' הקשה מ"א לדחות הרב"י שם דס"ל דמחיצות ב"ה הוי ההפסקה והרב"י ע"כ ס"ל דגם המקשן אסיק לחלק וכמו שדחה מ"א בסס"ק א' ראיית הרב"י מקושית הש"ס מרב' לרפרם ודו"ק:
machatzit_hashekel.en:
(siman kuf hei) Beit Av, etc. And behold Rashi, etc. And behold it is difficult for Rashi, etc. — for he did not write what Mordechai [wrote] at a distance of four amot, for Rashi also wrote thus; and what compelled Rashi is because it was difficult for Rashi why he challenged, etc.; and since perforce according to the presumption Rephaim meant at a distance of four amot even though he said plainly — from this Mordechai was born, that also according to the conclusion one may say thus under compulsion, as Magen Avraham wrote after this, even though Rephaim said plainly — behold we see Rashi explained thus for the questioner and we do not consider it strained. Learn from this that inside it is forbidden — for he did not say "more," that even inside it is permitted; perforce "opposite it" and not inside it. It deals with an old one in which there is no feces — and this is the answer the gemara rejected, from R' Yehoshua: privy — they said that even when there is no feces in it.
And R' Yehoshua stands, etc. — meaning, how will Ravina answer the gemara's challenge from Rav Yosef? Therefore he said Ravina holds R' Yehoshua stands on the mishnah — meaning, in the mishnah it teaches the measure of distancing four amot, and Rav [Chisda] innovated specifically behind him, but before him one needs as far as his eyes can see; and since in the mishnah the measure of as far as his eyes can see was not mentioned, on this R' Yehoshua stands — that even when there is no feces in it, this measure of distancing is required, namely four amot; and regarding the measure of four amot it is equal whether there is feces in it or not; but regarding before him there is certainly a distinction between there being feces in it and not — when there is feces in it, distancing as far as his eyes can see is required, and when there is no feces in it, even before him four amot suffices. And if so, Rephaim's words that he said "a person stands opposite the privy" — one may say at a distance of four amot — and this is not strained, for also according to the questioner's view it must be so, as Rashi explained above. And what Magen Avraham wrote that he stands on the mishnah — even though in the mishnah he did not mention the law of privy but only the law of feces — nevertheless one may say: since in truth we hold a privy has the law of feces, it is well to say he refers to the measure mentioned in the mishnah regarding feces. Accordingly, it is impossible in a new one that inside it is permitted; perforce Rephaim deals with an old one in which there is no feces, and four amot suffices. With this, what Mordechai wrote is resolved: Rephaim said, etc., at a distance of four amot and reads, and he explained it in a privy in which there is no feces — for Mordechai ruled the inquiry leniently, as Magen Avraham wrote afterward; and if so, perforce it must be so as above — only that accordingly it should be asked: what did the gemara challenge initially, as it establishes Rephaim in a privy in which there is no feces, and R' Yirmiyah: privy — they said that even when there is no feces in it? Let us say R' Yehoshua stands on the mishnah and four amot suffices, and Rephaim too meant at a distance of four amot, as Magen Avraham wrote for Ravina; therefore one must say: since the questioner did not bring up distinguishing in a new one between inside and outside until they answered him — this is because he held there is no distinction in privy law: either it has full privy law and is forbidden even outside, or it has no privy law at all and even inside is permitted; and if so, likewise regarding an old one without feces he would not know to distinguish — for since it has the law of "there is feces in it" for distancing four amot, likewise it should have the law of "there is feces in it" for before him as far as his eyes can see. Mordechai's words according to Ravina — what Magen Avraham wrote that he holds R' Yehoshua requires only distancing four amot — are according to the conclusion, that also regarding a new one they distinguish between inside and outside (and four amot is the law of inside); likewise one may say for a privy in which there is no feces that it should have the law of "there is feces in it" only in part and not be equal in all its laws to "there is feces in it." And indeed according to the conclusion there is no need again to establish Rephaim specifically in a new one; likewise the questioner deals with an old one without feces — and it is also settled that which the gemara said only "since" — for there is no need to veer from the first presumption and it deals specifically in a new one, since there is another establishment in an old one without feces as above; and therefore it said only "and such is the gemara's flow everywhere." But it is still to be asked: who compelled Magen Avraham to write that Mordechai recorded the inquiry leniently? Perhaps he recorded it stringently, as most poskim hold — and nevertheless according to the conclusion he establishes Rephaim in an old one without feces at a distancing of four amot as above. One reason: for Mordechai wrote and explained it in a privy without feces — and this is not explicit so in the gemara; it is only that according to the conclusion one may establish Rephaim in an old one without feces. But it is not explicit so in the gemara; on the contrary, it somewhat implies the reverse; and further it is impossible that he ruled the inquiry stringently — and this is because it is a Torah doubt; if so, all the more since it is possible to say that also according to the conclusion the gemara's answer remains that Rephaim deals in a new one and in an old one without feces one must distance as far as his eyes can see — whence do we lighten from a doubt that without feces suffices even before him at four amot? Nevertheless he ruled the inquiry leniently; and if so, perforce Rephaim deals with an old one without feces, as above.
And it is as though explicit in the gemara that according to the conclusion Rephaim deals with an old one without feces; and if so, for us who hold the inquiry stringently out of doubt — if so, likewise one may say that also according to the conclusion the gemara's answer remains that Rephaim deals in a new one. But in an old one, even without feces, before him must be as far as his eyes can see, as it answered initially — whence would we find a new leniency without necessity? And it is still to be asked accordingly: perforce the questioner did not bring up in his mind distinguishing the laws of privy, and he held in every matter either it has full privy law with all its stringencies or it has no privy law at all; if so, what does Magen Avraham challenge in siman kuf alef? See Magen Avraham, and such are his words: and if he has partitions — it is forbidden to recite inside it even from new. If so, what does the gemara challenge — that perhaps Rav Chisda deals, etc., and Ravina, etc.? Behold the questioner held: if inside is forbidden, outside too is forbidden; and if so, it would be that Rav Chisda deals without partitions — nevertheless it is fit to forbid as far as his eyes can see, like the law of an old privy — for the questioner held one may not distinguish privy laws as above. One reason that here Magen Avraham wrote he is inclined to explain Mordechai's words as we explained, not like the Ri; but in siman kuf alef Magen Avraham challenged to reject the Ri there, for he holds privy partitions are the interruption, and the Ri perforce holds the questioner too brought up distinguishing, as Magen Avraham rejected in siman kuf alef the Ri's proof from the gemara's challenge from Rava to Rephaim; examine carefully.
